title: Partitioning data
summary: Split records across shards using a clear key. Trace a simple remainder rule, then check hot keys, cross-shard work, and the cost of moving data.
introduction: A large library may keep shelves in several rooms. A sign tells each visitor which room holds a book. Partitioning data does something similar: a rule tells the app which storage part holds a record.
learningObjectives: Explain a partition key and a shard
Identify hot keys and operations that cross shards

blocks.text: A **partition** holds part of the data. When those parts live on separate storage servers, people often call them **shards**. A **partition key** is the value used to choose the part.

A useful key spreads both stored data and request work. Equal record counts do not guarantee equal traffic. One very popular book can create a **hot key**: one key receiving much more work than others.

Some systems split by ranges, such as book IDs 1 to 1000 and 1001 to 2000. Others apply a hash, a repeatable mixing rule, before picking a shard. This lesson uses a very small remainder rule so we can work it out by hand.

items: For each numeric book ID, compute ID remainder 3.
Book 10 goes to shard 1 because 10 divided by 3 leaves 1.
Book 13 also goes to shard 1. The app must use the same rule when it reads either book.

blocks.text: This small JavaScript model runs in the playground. Its numbers and events are chosen for learning. It does not create servers or measure a real service.

blocks.title: Partitioning data model
Expected result
blocks.content:
book 10: shard 1
book 11: shard 2
book 12: shard 0
book 13: shard 1

blocks.text: This model assumes nonnegative integer IDs. It demonstrates routing, not a production sharding library. Changing shardCount can move many IDs, so existing records need a safe migration plan.
Partitioning splits data. Replication copies data. A large system may use both: several shards, each with its own replicas and backups.

rows: Nearby key values can be read together
A busy newest range may receive most of the writes
Can spread many distinct keys more evenly
Range searches may need to ask several shards
Can make some local operations simpler
One large or busy group may overload its shard

blocks.text: A report across all books may need answers from every shard. A transaction that changes records on different shards also needs a clear agreement rule; it is harder than one local change.
If one popular book dominates traffic, adding shards may not spread that single key. A cache, separate read copies, or a different data model may help, depending on the job.

items: Change shardCount to 4. Predict where book 12 goes and whether book 10 moves.
Book 12 still goes to shard 0, but book 10 moves from shard 1 to shard 2. Changing the rule requires moving or locating existing data safely.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not change the shard rule while leaving old records behind without a routing and migration plan. A correct new calculation can still point to the wrong place for old data.
